worksheet.title: Change the Shape
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read & alter code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can change a loop to make Bit draw a different shape.

parts.title: Same loop, new shape
text: Bit's square uses range(4) and right 90. To draw a different shape, you change TWO things: how many sides (the range number) and the turn (given to you).
Read the chart — each shape just needs a different range and turn.

parts.title: Bit's square (start here)
parts.output: A square. Change range and the turn to get other shapes.

parts.caption: Change range() and the given turn → triangle, pentagon, or hexagon.

parts.title: Read it
parts.prompt: A triangle has 3 sides and the turn is 120 (given). What range number do you use? range(______)  and  right(______)

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: You change Bit's square to range(6) with right(60). PREDICT: how many sides will the shape have, and what is it called? Then run it.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Finish the code so Bit draws a TRIANGLE (the turn 120 is given):  for i in range(______):  bit.forward(50)  bit.right(120)

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit's loop is range(5) with right(72). How many sides does the shape have, and what is it called? (Hint: count the repeats.)

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: The range number sets how many sides; the turn is given for each shape. Change those two numbers and you change the shape Bit draws.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 3 · Intro Python Turtle
teacher_guide.title: Change the Shape
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students take a square's instructions and change two numbers — how many times it repeats and the turn — to draw a different shape (triangle, hexagon, pentagon). The turn for each shape is given. Change the numbers, change the shape. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start — showing the drawing (optional)
text: The worksheet shows the typed instructions AND a picture of each shape, so you can teach straight from the printout — no computer required.

To show it live (optional): open a browser, go to a free "Python turtle" playground (e.g. search "trinket python turtle"), type the few lines from the worksheet, and press Run — a turtle draws it. You only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Start from the square (repeat 4, turn 90). Change it to repeat 3 with turn 120 and run the triangle.
2. Show the turn chart: square 90, triangle 120, pentagon 72, hexagon 60. The repeat number = the number of sides; the turn is given per shape.
3. Let them work. Students do Exercises 1–4, solo or in pairs.
4. Wrap up: the repeat number sets the number of sides; the turn is given for each shape.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing the repeat number but forgetting the turn must match the shape.
Make it easier: give the turn and have students supply just the repeat number.
Make it harder: ask the repeat number and turn for a hexagon (repeat 6, turn 60).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The student matches a shape to its repeat number (Ex 1, 3), predicts the shape after changing the numbers (Ex 2), and names a polygon from the instructions (Ex 4).
